'''waif-pole''' (wāf′pōl), ''n.'' The pole to which the masthead waif is made fast.

'''waift†''', ''n.'' [Early mod. E., < ME. ''weft;'' a var. of ''waif'', with excrescent ''t:'' see ''waif.''] Same as ''waif''.
{{smaller block|<poem>For that a ''waift'', the which by fortune came
Upon your seas, he claym’d as propertie.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. xii. 31.}}}}

'''wail<sup>1</sup>''' (wāl), ''v.'' [< ME. ''wailen'', ''waillen'', ''weilen'', ''weylen'', < Icel. ''væla'', ''vala'', mod. ''vola'', wail, < ''væ! vei!'' interj., woe! see ''woe''. Cf. ''bewail.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To express sorrow by a mournful inarticulate vocal sound; lament; moan; cry plaintively.
{{smaller block|<poem>I mot wepe and ''weyle'' whyl I live.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 437.}}
<poem>The melancholy days are come, the saddest of the year,
Of ''wailing'' winds, and naked woods, and meadows brown and sere.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Death of the Flowers.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To grieve over; lament; bemoan; bewail.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou holy chirche, thou maist be ''wailed''.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 6271.}}
<poem>Tell these sad women
’Tis fond to ''wail'' inevitable strokes,
As ’tis to laugh at them.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iv. 1. 26.}}}}

'''wail<sup>1</sup>''' (wāl), ''n.'' [< ''wail<sup>1</sup>'', ''v.''] The act of lamenting aloud; wailing; a moan; a plaintive cry or sound.
{{smaller block|<poem>From its rocky caverns the deep-voiced neighboring ocean
Speaks, and in accents disconsolate answers the ''wail'' of the forest.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Evangeline, ii. 5.}}
<poem>The dead, whose dying eyes
Were closed with ''wail''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, xc.}}}}

'''wagtail''' (wag′tāl), ''v. i.''   [< ''wagtail, n.'']   To flutter; move the wings and tail like a wagtail. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>A payr of busie chattering Pies, . . .
From bush to bush ''wag-tayling'' here and there.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Trophies.}}}}

'''wagwant''' (wag′wônt), ''n.'' Same as ''wag-wanton.''

'''wag-wanton''' (wag′wôn-tọn), ''n.'' The quaking-grass, ''Briza media.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''wag-wit''' (wag′wit), ''n.'' A wag; a would-be wit.
{{smaller block|All the ''wag-wits'' in the highway are grinning in applause of the ingenious rogue. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 354.}}}}

'''wah''' (wä), ''n.''   [Native name.]   The panda, ''Ælurus fulgens'', of the Himalayan region. See cut under ''panda''.

'''Wahabi, Wahabee''' (wä-hä′bē), ''n.''   [< Ar. ''Wahhabī'', < ''Wahhab'' (see def.).]   One of the followers of Abd-el-Wahhab (1691–1787), a Mohammedan reformer, who opposed all practices not sanctioned by the Koran. {{smaller|His successors formed a powerful dominion, whose chief seat was in Nejd in central Arabia. They were overthrown by Ibrahim Pasha in 1818, but afterward regained much of their former power in central Arabia. Also ''Wahabite.''}}
{{smaller block|A sect of Muhammadan puritans, known as ''Wahabis'', who affect a strict and ascetic way of life, such as prevailed in the time of the Prophet, and denounce all commentaries on the Koran, and all such modern innovations as the worship of relics.
{{right|''J. T. Wheeler'', Short Hist. India, p. 668.}}}}

'''Wahabiism''' (wä-hä′bē-izm), ''n.''   [< ''Wahabi'' + ''-ism.'']   The doctrines, principles, or practices of the Wahabis. ''W. G. Palgrave.''

'''Wahabite''' (wä-hä′bīt), ''n.''   [< ''Wahabi'' + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.]   Same as ''Wahabi. Laboulaye.''

'''wahahe''' (wä-hä′hā), ''n.''   [Maori.]   A tree, ''Dysoxylum'' (''Hartighsea'') ''spectabile'', found in New Zealand. {{smaller|It has a height of 40 or 50 feet, and bears panicles of pale-colored flowers from 8 to 12 inches long, pendulous from the trunk and main branches. Its leaves are said to be used by the natives like hops, and an infusion of them as a stomachic. Also ''kohe.''}}

'''Waha Lake trout.''' See ''trout''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wahoo''' (wȧ-hö′), ''n.''   [Amer. Ind.]   '''1.''' A North American shrub, the burning-bush, ''Euonymus atropurpureus'', ornamental in autumn for its pendulous capsules, revealing in dehiscence the bright-scarlet arils of its seeds. Its bark is the officinal euonymus, credited with cholagogic and laxative properties.—'''2.''' The bearberry of the Pacific United States, ''Rhamnus Purshiana'', the source of cascara sagrada, perhaps so called from its medicinal affinity to the former.—'''3.''' The winged elm, ''Ulmus alata'', a small tree with corky winged branches, found southward in the United States. {{smaller|The wood is unwedgeable, and is largely used for hubs, blocks, etc. The name has also been applied to ''Tilia heterophylla'' (see ''Tilia'') and to the Japanese quince (which see, under ''quince''<sup>1</sup>).}}

Also written ''waahoo'' (this form being sometimes used distinctively in sense 1) and ''whahoo''.

'''waid†, waide†.''' Obsolete spellings of the preterit and past participle of ''weigh''<sup>1</sup>.

'''waif''' (wāf), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [Formerly also ''waive'' (from the plural), also ''waift'' (see ''waive'', ''n.'', ''waift''); < ME. ''waif'', ''weif'', ''weife'' (pl. ''wayves'', ''weyves''), < OF. ''waif'', ''wef'', ''gueyf'', ''gaif'', fem. ''waive'', ''gaive'' (pl. ''waives'', ''gaives''), a waif (''choses gaives'', things lost and not claimed), < Icel. ''veif'', anything waving or flapping about, ''veifan'', a moving about uncertainly, ''veifa'', vibrate, waver: see ''waive''.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' Anything blown by the wind or drifted in by the ocean; a thing tossed abroad and abandoned; a stray or odd piece or article.
{{smaller block|''Weifes'', things forsaken, miscarried, or lost.
{{right|''Cotgrave'', 1611.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Rolling in his mind
Old ''waifs'' of rhyme.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', The Brook.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''law'': (''a'') Goods found of which the owner is not known. {{smaller block|Of wardes and of wardemotes, ''wayues'' and strayues.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), i. 92.}}}}
(''b'') Such goods as a thief, when pursued, throws away to prevent being apprehended.
{{smaller block|''Waifs'' . . . are goods stolen, and waved or thrown away by the thief in his flight, for fear of being apprehended.
{{right|''Blackstone'', Com., I. viii.}}}}
'''3.''' A wanderer; one who is lost; a neglected, homeless wretch: applied also to beasts.
{{smaller block|<poem>Virtue and vice had bound’ries in old time; . . .
’Twas hard perhaps on here and there a ''waif'',
Desirous to return, and not receiv’d.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iii. 80.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh a’ ye pious, godly flocks, . . .
Wha now will keep ye frae the fox, . . .
Or wha will tent the ''waifs'' and crocks
About the dykes! ''Burns'', The Twa Herds.</poem>}}
'''4.''' Same as ''weft'' or ''waft''.
{{smaller block|The officer who first discovers it [a whale] sets a ''waif'' (a small flag) in his boat, and gives chase.
{{right|''C. M. Scammon'', Marine Mammals, p. 25.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Masthead waif''', a light pole, six or eight feet long, with a hoop covered with canvas at the end: used by whalemen in signaling boats. Compare ''waft'', ''n.'', 4.}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Vagabond; worthless; ignoble; inferior. Also ''waff''. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|And the Lord King forbids that any ''waif'' (i. e. vagabond) or unknown (“uncuth”) man be entertained anywhere except in a borough, and there only for one night, unless he or his horse be detained there by sickness so that an essoign [valid excuse by reason of sickness or infirmity] can be shown. ''Laws of Hen. II.'', quoted in Ribton-Turner’s
{{right|[Vagrants and Vagrancy, p. 26.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And wull and ''waif'' for eight lang years
They sail’d upon the sea.</poem>
{{right|''Rosmer Hafmand'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 253).}}}}

'''waif-pole''' (wāf′pōl), ''n.'' The pole to which the masthead waif is made fast.
